title: Extraterrestrial fireworks
caption: Supernova remnant E0102 in the Small Magellanic Cloud, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
captureDate: Hubble ACS data 2003; WFPC2 oxygen images 1995

celestial: 1E 0102.2-7219, E0102 · constellation Tucana · about 200000 light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: Published in the ESA/Hubble image archive. No published rating.

story: A greenish-blue shell of debris sits just below the center of this Hubble image, much like fireworks. It is E0102, formally 1E0102.2-7219, what remains after a massive star exploded as a supernova in the Small Magellanic Cloud, a nearby dwarf galaxy. In the upper right glows the star-forming region N 76, a delicate structure in lavender and peach hues.
The two look different because of what they are made of. N 76 shines mainly with glowing hydrogen. E0102 is an oxygen-rich remnant, with a great deal of oxygen and very little hydrogen or helium.

One explanation is that the star that exploded had already blown most of its hydrogen away in a stellar wind. It may have been a Wolf-Rayet star, a type that can be upward of 20 times the Sun's mass and famous for strong winds, which strip away outer shells and leave oxygen behind.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (3.01 x 2.41 arcminutes) and distance (200000 light years), the frame spans roughly 175 × 140 light-years. Its light set out about 200,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image combines 2003 data from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, through blue, visible, infrared and hydrogen filters, with oxygen images from the Wide Field Planetary Camera 2. The color assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: Narrow filters isolate the glow of specific gases like oxygen and hydrogen, so the colors map chemistry more than what an eye would see.

explore: E0102 is only about 2000 years old, young enough that astronomers can study material from a massive star's core directly. It lies almost 50 light-years from the edge of N 76.
The Small Magellanic Cloud is visible from the Southern Hemisphere toward Tucana and lies roughly 210,000 light-years away.
